extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing criteria and conceptual standards Thomas Kuhn uses to characterize paradigms, normal science, and scientific revolutions — i.e., what counts as data, measurement, and explanation across paradigm change. Useful for evaluating accounts of scientific practice and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms determine perception (what scientists 'see')
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientist who embraces a new paradigm finds the same constellation of objects transformed; paradigms determine large areas of experience so that observers literally 'see' different phenomena (e.g., planets, pendulums, condensers, oxygen) when looking at the same sorts of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: after Copernicus astronomers 'saw' new celestial bodies; Lavoisier 'saw' oxygen where Priestley saw dephlogisticated air; Galileo saw a pendulum where Aristotelians saw constrained fall. Paradigm-induced gestalt switches change which aspects of the world are salient and thereby what regularities are accessible to inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science is paradigm-driven and interpretive
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science aims to refine, extend, and articulate an already accepted paradigm; it presupposes what counts as a datum, which instruments to use, and which concepts are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a paradigm the scientist 'knew what a datum was, what instruments might be used to retrieve it, and what concepts were relevant to its interpretation.' Most research is interpretive work that articulates the paradigm rather than questions it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms are not corrigible by normal science
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science cannot correct a paradigm; it can only lead to recognition of anomalies and to crises which may then be terminated by a revolutionary event (a gestalt switch) rather than by piecemeal interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science ultimately leads to anomalies and crises. Termination of a crisis typically occurs through a relatively sudden and unstructured event like the 'scales falling from the eyes' or a 'lightning flash,' not through normal interpretive procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and observations are themselves paradigm-dependent (not unequivocally stable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data that scientists collect are different across paradigms because what counts as the relevant features of experience depends on paradigm commitments; a pendulum is not the same datum as constrained fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a pendulum and constrained fall are different perceptual/conceptual objects, the measurements and indices relevant to each are different. Regularities accessible under one paradigm may not be exemplified under another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory operations and measurements are selected and paradigm-determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations and measurements are not 'the given' but are collected and selected for scrutiny because they promise fruitful elaboration of the accepted paradigm; different paradigms engage different laboratory manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operations are 'the collected with difficulty.' The measurements to be performed on a pendulum are not those relevant to constrained fall. After a revolution many old measurements become irrelevant and are replaced by others, though some manipulations may persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempts at a neutral observation-language presuppose a paradigm and fail to be truly neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to construct a pure observation-language presuppose a paradigm (a current theory or everyday discourse) and thus embody expectations about nature; such languages function only within the domain already known and break down when expectations are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts that eliminate non-logical and non‑perceptual terms still 'embody a host of expectations about nature' and 'fail the moment these expectations are violated.' Nelson Goodman is cited to show limits of such restricted languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm change reorganizes entire related domains simultaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning a new scientific concept or paradigm entails a holistic reorganization: many related phenomena are seen differently at once (not item-by-item), so the scientist's perceived world and expectations change together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a child learning 'mama' or Copernicans redefining 'planet' — to see oxygen instead of dephlogisticated air involves changing how many related chemical phenomena are classified and investigated simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some instruments and language persist across paradigms but their role and results may change
rubrics_metrics.description: After a scientific revolution many of the same manipulations, instruments, and terms remain, but their relation to the paradigm or their concrete results can differ; the same operation can become an index to a different aspect of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: eighteenth-century chemical operations that were interpreted via affinity theory later took on different significance under Dalton's atomic theory; some enduring manipulations in postrevolutionary science are performed with the same instruments but reinterpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation presupposes paradigm and cannot by itself bring about paradigm change
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists interpret observations as part of normal science within a paradigm; interpretation presupposes relevant concepts and cannot by itself correct or replace the paradigm that frames it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galileo's, Aristotle's, Musschenbroek's, and Franklin's interpretations of phenomena all presupposed paradigms. Interpretation articulates a paradigm but does not explain the sudden intuitive reorganization (gestalt) that produces a new paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm shifts often involve non‑piecemeal, intuitive insights (gestalt switches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary change is often achieved by sudden, holistic intuitions that gather up large portions of prior experience and transform them into a new bundle of experience linked to the new paradigm; these are not ordinary interpretive steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'flashes of intuition' depend upon accumulated experience with the old paradigm but are not logically linked to particular items of that experience; they enable new puzzles to be seen and solved in ways that deliberative interpretation cannot produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational criteria (e.g., definitions or tests) depend on paradigm and may not exist prior to paradigm change
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctions that later seem operational (e.g., mixture vs compound) were not always separable by tests in earlier paradigms; operational definitions presuppose the conceptual framework that renders them sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eighteenth-century chemists often treated solutions as compounds under affinity theory because operational tests separating mixtures and compounds were not recognized or sought; Dalton's atomic theory later created anomalies and new operational criteria.
